idiom_name: typed module-scope cell with ??= (or a memoised promise)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no concurrency semantics to JavaScript, so the realization is the same module-scope cell with a type the compiler can check: `let config: Config | undefined` plus `config ??= buildConfig()` gives one initialisation per module instance, and an async cell typed as `Promise<Config>` memoises the in-flight operation so concurrent callers await the same work. Module-level `const` remains the honest answer for values cheap enough to build at import time, and typing the cell as non-optional after initialisation is what keeps the fast path readable. The classic lock-and-flag structure stays justified only around real shared memory - worker threads with SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics - which TypeScript types but does not abstract; a plain object cell cannot be shared across workers at all, because each worker gets its own module instance.
pitfalls: Types are erased: nothing prevents two module instances (worker thread, duplicated bundle, per-request loader) from holding two different cells, so a type-level singleton is not a runtime guarantee.
??= treats a legitimately undefined value as unset, and a cached rejected promise makes the failure permanent unless the cell is cleared explicitly.
Class-field initialisers and top-level side effects reintroduce eager evaluation: keep the build inside the accessor or behind a getter.
Under strict concurrency the module-scope cell is shared mutable state across async tasks; if the initialiser awaits I/O, two callers can interleave unless the promise (not the value) is memoised.
